items.title: A l'entrada del tens clar
items.subtitle: At the coming of the bright season: troubadour round dance
items.source: Pierre Aubry, Trouvères et troubadours (Paris: Félix Alcan, 1909), pp. 60-61, from the chansonnier of Saint-Germain-des-Prés (Paris, BnF fr. 20050)

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of Aubry, Trouvères et troubadours (1909), at p. 60
the same, p. 61 (the refrain and verses II-III)

items.blocked: Source check: compare with Aubry pp. 60-61, especially the first note of the refrain's second line (an F sharp: the head sits high, but its sharp is on the F space and the cadence G-F sharp-G wants it), the grace notes, and the second "E-ya!" (B, G, A, not B, c, d like the other two). Classroom check: the class as chorus (the "E-ya!" answers and the refrain), a soloist or the teacher on the verse lines, and a round dance in a circle.
items.notes: THE WORDS, verse I (sung): "A l'entrada del tems clar, - Eya, / Per joia recomençar, - Eya, / E per jelos irritar, - Eya, / Vol la regina mostrar / Qu'el es si amorosa. / Alavi', alavia, jelos, / Laissaz nos, laissaz nos / Ballar entre nos, entre nos." At the coming of the bright season, to begin the joy again and to annoy the jealous, the queen wants to show that she is so full of love. Away, away, jealous ones, let us, let us dance among ourselves.

dossier.function: A round dance for the coming of spring: the "April queen" calls everyone, girl and boy, to come and dance, to spite the jealous old king; the chorus shouts "Eya!" after each of the soloist's lines and sings the refrain, "Away, away, jealous ones, let us dance among ourselves."
dossier.elements: Call and answer: a soloist's line (always the same seven notes, B c d d d B A) and the chorus's "E-ya!" held over four bars; then a sixteen-bar refrain for everyone. 3/4 in a long-short swing (half then quarter), the medieval first rhythmic mode as Aubry read it; G is the final, the range an octave (F sharp to e).
dossier.practice: Vif (Aubry). A soloist and a chorus, as the plate marks them; danced in a ring. The band plays only a tabor-like drum (ours); the plate has the voice alone.
dossier.honesty: Anonymous, 12th-13th century, from the chansonnier of Saint-Germain-des-Prés (Paris, BnF fr. 20050), which writes no rhythm; the 3/4 long-short rhythm, the grace notes and the two F sharps are Aubry's reading (1909). The drum is ours.
dossier.licence: Pierre Aubry (1874-1910), Trouvères et troubadours (Paris: Félix Alcan, 1909): public domain in the US, Canada and Europe (Aubry d. 1910).
dossier.respect: A secular spring dance; the "jealous" are the old husband and his kind, a stock figure of the genre. Nothing sacred.
dossier.review: An early-music singer, for the Occitan words and the rhythm.

items.title: Arirang
items.subtitle: Korean folk song, as Hulbert wrote it down in 1896
items.source: Homer B. Hulbert, "Korean Vocal Music", The Korean Repository 3 (Seoul: Trilingual Press, February 1896), p. 51; archive.org, University of Illinois copy

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of The Korean Repository vol. 3 (1896); the article is pp. 45-53 (may not be the Illinois copy the notes name)

items.blocked: Confirm bar 2's rhythm (the print shows no flags; read as quavers to match bar 1 and fill the bar), and have a Korean culture bearer hear it with the janggu.
items.notes: The oldest written Arirang. Hulbert's romanisation is kept (A-ra-rung for Arirang); in today's spelling the words are "Arirang arirang arariyo, arirang eolsa bae ddiwora. Mungyeong saejae bakdal namu, hongdukkae bangmang-i da naganda": the birch trees of Mungyeong pass all go to make washing clubs. Bar 2 has no flags in the print; it is read as bar 1 (two quavers and a minim), which fills the bar.

dossier.function: folk song (minyo); the "Mungyeong Saejae" Arirang, which Hulbert heard everywhere in Seoul in 1896; the chorus is fixed and the verses are improvised
dossier.elements: 3/4 (Hulbert's notation of a lilting triple metre, the semachi jangdan); five notes, G A C D E, ending on G; the chorus "Arirang, arirang, arariyo" then a verse about the birch trees of Mungyeong Saejae made into washing clubs
dossier.practice: moderate and swaying; a singer leads the verse and everyone sings the chorus; the janggu drum keeps the jangdan; the band holds an open fifth on G with a janggu-like pattern on the kick and rim
dossier.honesty: arranged: the melody and Hulbert's romanised words as he printed them; the drone and drum pattern are ours, after the semachi jangdan as commonly taught
dossier.licence: public domain (Homer B. Hulbert, "Korean Vocal Music", The Korean Repository 3, February 1896, pp. 45-53; Hulbert died 1949); read bar by bar from the archive.org scan of the University of Illinois copy on 2026-11-10
dossier.respect: Arirang is a national song of Korea, North and South, and on UNESCO's list (2012, 2014); present it as a living song with many regional versions, this one as the earliest written down, by an American missionary
dossier.review: a Korean culture bearer or a teacher of gugak before publishing

items.title: B'qāw ʿala khēr
items.subtitle: Stay well: the Maghreb's closing song
items.source: Jules Rouanet, "La musique arabe dans le Maghreb", Lavignac, Encyclopédie de la musique, Part I vol. 5 (1922), p. 2824

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of Lavignac, Encyclopédie de la musique, Part I vol. 5 (1922), p. 2824 (Rouanet, "La musique arabe dans le Maghreb")

performanceNotes: No recording found yet; the same places as Rāna jīnāk (AMAR; the Yafil 78s on Gallica). Listen before linking.
items.blocked: Source check: compare with Rouanet p. 2824, especially the naturals (E natural only where he marks one; the other E's are E flat by the key signature), the three half-bars of 3/8 he prints inside the 6/8, and the return to the sign. An Arabic speaker for the words. Classroom check: as the goodbye song, with a couplet for each child, as the tradition names each guest.
items.notes: THE PLATE: "M.M. dotted quarter = 108", 6/8, two flats, a sign (segno) after the pickup and a return to it at the end; three staves with words "B'kaou aâ la kheir! neb-ghi ne-rou-oua h' H'ass el moued-den fes-sa-ma-i ci Ah! Eb-kaou aâ la kheir!". Below, "Rythme d'accompagnement" in two lines of alternating eighths.

dossier.function: The closing song of every Maghreb feast: the musicians' leave-taking of the hosts who listened to them (Rouanet's footnote 2), "the obligatory conclusion of every feast, whatever its character, where there is any music at all". Every couplet begins "Stay in peace!"; when the traditional couplets run out, the singers improvise lines naming the guests and the people they wish to honour, rhyming the names with formulas of thanks.
dossier.elements: 6/8, dotted quarter = 108; a two-eighth pickup and three short phrases, ending on B flat and going back to the sign; key of two flats with E natural as a leading tone to F; range B flat to g.
dossier.practice: Sung by the musicians as they leave, the drums keeping the alternating rhythm. In class: the goodbye song at the end of a lesson, the first line sung by all, then couplets with each child's name, the way the singers name each guest.
dossier.accompaniment: Tradition (Rouanet pp. 2823-2824, 2838): the feast's musicians, indoors the women's ensemble with kamanja (violin), tar (jingled frame drum) and derbouka (goblet drum); outdoors ghaita with drums. Rouanet's printed "rythme d'accompagnement" alternates a high stroke and a low stroke by eighths: high on 1, 3 and 5, low on 2, 4 and 6 of the 6/8 bar. Band here: high on rim, low on bd, his rhythm exactly; barred in 3/8, the pattern alternates bar by bar. No bass or chords. Needs: derbouka, tar, kamanja.
dossier.lyrics: Rouanet prints the first couplet: "B'kaou aâ la kheir! nebghi nerououah', h'ass el moueddén fes-samai ... Ah! Ebkaou aâ la kheir!": tentatively بقاو على خير، نبغي نروّح، حسّ المؤذّن في السما, "Stay well! I want to go home: the muezzin's voice is in the sky (it is dawn) ... Ah! Stay well!" Fit for class; the muezzin line marks the hour the feast ends. The class couplets with names are the tradition's own practice (footnote 2). The Arabic script and translation wait for an Arabic speaker.
dossier.honesty: Traditional, anonymous; notes, words and rhythm as Rouanet printed them (1920), barred here in 3/8 (his 6/8 bars are pairs of these) so that the three half-bars he prints need no change of metre; the small notes before his sign are the pickup, written here once at the start.
dossier.licence: Jules Rouanet (1858-1944), in Lavignac, Encyclopédie de la musique, Part I vol. 5 (Paris: Delagrave, 1922; section copyright 1920): public domain in the US and in Canada (Rouanet d. 1944).
dossier.respect: The words mention the muezzin's call, as the sign that night is over; nothing in the song is a religious text. Rouanet's framing is a colonial scholar's; the record keeps his facts about the music.
dossier.review: An Arabic speaker familiar with Algerian song, for the words and the class couplets.

items.title: Cha-ko'mba, ko'mba
items.subtitle: Hopping song: Ndau children's game
items.source: Natalie Curtis Burlin, Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent (New York: G. Schirmer, 1920), Children's Songs II, p. 106 (game notes p. 31)

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent, at p. 106

items.blocked: Source check: compare with Curtis p. 106 (Children's Songs II). Classroom check: a hopping race on one leg in time to the song, in a space where that is safe.
items.notes: THE GAME (Curtis, p. 31): "In the evening the children play this singing-game, while hopping on one leg in time to the music to a given goal in a hopping race. They must always hop on one leg, for to put down the other foot would be to lose the race."

dossier.function: A singing game for the evening: the children hop on one leg in time to the song, racing to a goal. Putting the other foot down loses the race (Curtis, p. 31, from Simango).
dossier.elements: Three notes (F, A flat, B flat: la, do, re), two bars sung twice: four quick eighths and a held note, then a stressed note, a rest and the answer. 3/4, with a repeat.
dossier.practice: Rather quickly (quarter = 116, Curtis). Sung while hopping, one hop to a beat; the band plays only a soft low thump on each beat for the hops.
dossier.honesty: Traditional; the notes and words as Curtis printed them from C. Kamba Simango's singing; the English line is Curtis's. The thump on the beat is ours, for the hops; the plate has the voice alone.
dossier.licence: Natalie Curtis Burlin (d. 1921), Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent (G. Schirmer, 1920): public domain in the US and in Canada (Simango d. 1966, out of copyright under the life-plus-50 term then in force).
dossier.respect: A children's game, nothing sacred. Credit C. Kamba Simango. Curtis notes that the "th" of m'nthalila is not pronounced as in English and that the t is followed by a breathed h.
dossier.review: A Chindau speaker, for the words.

items.title: Galloway road
items.subtitle: Jamaican ring game
items.source: Walter Jekyll (ed.), Jamaican Song and Story (London: David Nutt, 1907), Project Gutenberg #35410 (music as MusicXML), no. XCVIII, p. 199

sourceUrls.label: Project Gutenberg #35410: Jamaican Song and Story, with page images and the music

items.blocked: Have a Jamaican culture bearer hear it; check whether the class version should pass stones (as in Manuel Road) or choose partners, as Jekyll describes.
items.notes: Words and tune as Jekyll printed them (Allegretto). "I go to Galloway road (where there is a quarry). Girls and boys are breaking stones. They break them one by one, two by two... Choosing stones suggests choosing partners."

dossier.function: game: a ring game about breaking stones on the Galloway road quarry; choosing stones stands for choosing partners. A relative of the stone-passing song "Go Dung a Manuel Road"
dossier.elements: 2/4 with triplets on "Galloway" and "Take up the one that you"; the refrain "gal an' boy" on a falling F D D D; the raised G sharp leading to A in bar 3
dossier.practice: Allegretto; leader and ring sing together; in class it works as a stone or bean-bag passing game on the beat (a later practice, not Jekyll's description)
dossier.honesty: arranged: melody and words as Jekyll printed them; mento backing ours
dossier.licence: public domain (published 1907; Project Gutenberg: for the use of anyone anywhere); notes converted from Gutenberg's MusicXML and checked bar by bar against its page image on 2026-11-10
dossier.respect: a work and play song; the words describe convict and labourer stone-breaking, worth a sentence of history in class
dossier.review: a Jamaican culture bearer (a teacher of Jamaican folk song, or the Jamaica Memory Bank / Louise Bennett's recordings) before publishing

items.title: Gurkha dance tune
items.subtitle: Gurkha dance, four men clapping (one bar, repeated)
items.source: Fox Strangways, The Music of Hindostan (1914), Ex. 127, p. 57

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of The Music of Hindostan, at p. 57

items.blocked: Read the one bar again at 2400 dpi (p. 57, scan p. 79, first staff): the grouping of beats 1 and 3 (eighth plus two sixteenths, or a triplet) and the end of beat 0 (G c and a rest); then source-check.
items.notes: "To such tunes as" this, four men A, B, C, D danced, lifting the foot to the level of the knee, their movements on the four beats of the bar, which the plate numbers 1 2 3 0 (0 is the silent beat): (1) all clap hands; (2) B and D touch right palm to A and C's left palm, fingers pointing upwards; (3) clap hands; (0) D and B touch left palm to A and C's right palm, and all step backwards instead of forwards on this beat. No words, no tempo and no tonic are printed; no signature, and the notes are d, c and G, so the drone is on G and the band's clap line marks the three hand-beats and leaves beat 0 silent.
items.kindNote: One bar, which four men repeated while they clapped and danced (the moves are in the N: line). It would want the clap pattern as a rhythm part, the dance as steps for the class, and how many times round it went.

items.title: Gurkha sing-song
items.subtitle: Gurkha song, danced, with drum
items.source: Fox Strangways, The Music of Hindostan (1914), Ex. 129, p. 57

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of The Music of Hindostan, at p. 57

items.blocked: Source check: hear it against the plate (p. 57, scan p. 79) and confirm the three things a measurement cannot settle: the "w" over the e in the solo (read as an upper mordent), the right hand on the high head of the drum, and that the unlabelled first staff belongs to the same song as the solo and chorus.
items.notes: From a sing-song of the men of the 2nd Goorkhas after a hockey match: the songs followed so fast that no words could be taken down; one or two men whirled in the middle of the crowd with bent knees and elbows and upturned palms, a couple of bars at a time danced crouching, and at the end of a chorus there was sometimes a grunted "Ha! Ha!".

items.title: Gurkha song, first version
items.subtitle: Gurkha song, four versions sung in turn
items.source: Fox Strangways, The Music of Hindostan (1914), Ex. 130, pp. 57-58

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of The Music of Hindostan, at p. 57

items.blocked: Check both bars against the plate (p. 57, scan p. 79, last staff): the lengths in bar 1 (read one eighth short) and bar 2 (read two eighths short); then read the 2nd, 3rd and 4th versions on p. 58 (scan p. 80) as variants.
items.notes: From the same sing-song as Ex. 129; the plate gives four versions of the one tune, the 1st here, the 2nd to 4th on p. 58, which shows how the men varied it. No tonic is marked and there is no signature; the notes are E d e c B, a Gurkha pentatonic shape on the fourth G-c or d-G (Fox Strangways groups Exs. 129, 130 and 137 as the plagal form, p. 70); the drone is on G. No words.
items.kindNote: The first of four versions of one tune that the men sang in turn; the 2nd to 4th (p. 58) show how they varied it. The four versions together, sung in turn, are the piece.

items.title: La Rana
items.subtitle: The frog: Mexican cumulative song
items.source: Eleanor Hague, Spanish-American Folk-Songs, Memoirs of the American Folk-Lore Society 10 (1917), No. 76, pp. 98-99

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of Hague, Spanish-American Folk-Songs (1917), at p. 98

items.blocked: Source check: compare with Hague No. 76, pp. 98-99, especially the last bar of the verse (two quarters on the plate, the second under a fermata, written here as a quarter and a held half) and the sixteenth pickup. Classroom check: how far down the chain to go (it ends with Death and God; a class may stop at the blacksmith), and how the chain fits the music, which the book does not write out.
items.notes: THE CHAIN (Hague, p. 99): "Each verse adds an animal, and the whole list is repeated." Verse 2: "La Rana se sale a pasear, / Viene el Raton y se trina, / El Raton, la Rana, la Araña, la Rana, / Cantando debajo del agua." The list: La Araña, la Rana; la Rana, el Raton; el Raton, el Gato; el Gato, el Perro; el Perro, el Palo; el Palo, la Lumbre; la Lumbre, el Agua; el Agua, el Buey; el Buey, el Cochino; el Cochino, el Herrero; el Herrero, la Muerte; la Muerte, Dios. In English: the spider and the frog, the frog and the rat, the rat and the cat, the cat and the dog, the dog and the stick, the stick and the light, the light and the water, the water and the ox, the ox and the pig, the pig and the blacksmith, the blacksmith and Death, Death and God.

dossier.function: A cumulative children's song: each verse brings a new creature or thing out to sing with the frog under the water, and the whole chain is sung back each time (spider, frog, rat, cat, dog, stick, fire, water, ox, pig, blacksmith, Death, God). It ends with everyone croaking "ga-ra, ga-ra", the last croak held as long as breath lasts.
dossier.elements: D major, 3/4, a range of a ninth (A below middle C to the B above it); quarters with one sixteenth pickup and one pair of eighths; the croaking coda in 2/4 on one note.
dossier.practice: The verse sung by everyone; the chain added verse by verse (a memory game); the "ga-ra" croaks ad lib, the last one held a long time (Hague's note).
dossier.honesty: Traditional; the notes, Spanish words and English singing translation as Hague printed them from Mrs. Dane Coolidge's singing. The fermata bar is lengthened to fill the metre (see the N: lines).
dossier.licence: Eleanor Hague (1875-1954), Spanish-American Folk-Songs, Memoirs of the American Folk-Lore Society 10 (1917): public domain in the US (published 1917) and in Canada (Hague d. 1954).
dossier.respect: A children's song; the chain ends "La Muerte, Dios" (Death, God), which a teacher may choose to sing or leave.
dossier.review: A Spanish-speaking teacher, for the words and the chain.

items.title: Mafuve
items.subtitle: Dance of girls: Ndau dance song with four clap parts
items.source: Natalie Curtis Burlin, Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent (New York: G. Schirmer, 1920), "Mafuve: Dance of Girls", pp. 103-105 (words and dance pp. 29-30)

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of Curtis, Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent (1920), p. 103 (music with the four clap parts; continues pp. 104-105)
the same, pp. 29-30: the dance, and the words with Curtis's translation

performanceNotes: No recording of this song found. Curtis made phonograph records of the singers (book, p. xxv), not yet located (Columbia University, the Library of Congress and the Smithsonian are the likely places). For the style of Ndau singing with clapping, the International Library of African Music (ILAM, Rhodes University) holds many Ndau recordings: digitalarchives.ru.ac.za, search "Ndau"; listen and choose one before linking.
items.blocked: Transcription: the opening six bars and the four clap parts are read; the rest of the song (pp. 104-105: "Ndo da kwumisha", the grunted "O ha o" bars, the ending) is still to transcribe, though Curtis says any phrase may be repeated and the order is free, so these six bars looped are already the song as danced. Then source check (the sextuplet clap figures, and "e" at the end of bar 4 against "e yo-we" at the start of bar 5), a Chindau speaker for the words, and a classroom try: four groups, one clap part each, two dancers stamping in the middle.
items.notes: THE CLAPS (p. 103), one bar each, in sixteenths of a 3/4 bar: 1. two eighths (accented) | an eighth-note triplet, the last tied over | a sextuplet: (tie), clap, (hold), clap, (hold), rest. 2. (the dancers only) rest, clap, rest, clap | rest | rest. 3. four sixteenths | a sextuplet: eighth, eighth, sixteenth, sixteenth | two eighths. 4. eighth and two sixteenths | sixteenth, eighth, two thirty-seconds | three sixteenths and a rest. A footnote gives a quintuplet as another rhythm for beats 2 and 3 of the third part.

dossier.function: A dance song of girls and young women (Ndau, central Mozambique). It tells of a young bride who, though she loves her husband and her new home, longs for her mother and her childhood home: "Alas, my mother's home! I left my mother's home; I love my husband's home." Two girls dance at a time, facing each other, starting with two stamps; the others stand round them in a circle, clapping and singing, until their turn (Curtis pp. 29-30, from C. Kamba Simango).
dossier.elements: 3/4 at quarter = 63; E major; each bar a call on the first beat ("E-yo-we", "Kwa-mai-we") then a quick falling run of vocables (F E D C C: "we yo we i-ye"); the first beat carries the words and the dancers' two stamps, the rest is "parenthetical", carried by quicker clapping (Curtis's note under the music). Range B below middle C to B.
dossier.practice: Not fast. The song is repeated and recombined at will: "any phrase or group of phrases of this song may be repeated an indefinite number of times, so the song may be sung for an hour, or an hour and a half, steadily. There is no prescribed order" (Curtis, p. 105). In class: four groups take one clap rhythm each, two dancers stamp on the first beat and do the second clap; everyone sings.
dossier.accompaniment: Tradition: "No drums are used, the song being accompanied by the clapping of hands" (p. 29). Curtis prints four hand-clap rhythms under the voice and explains (p. 105) that no one keeps one rhythm all through: each clapper changes every two or three bars, but "a chorus of clapping, composed of all four rhythms sounding at the same time, is always heard" once the song is under way. The second rhythm (16th rest, clap, 16th rest, clap on the first beat) belongs to the two dancers. Band here: the four rhythms exactly as printed, each on its own sound so the layers can be told apart (clap, claves, wood block, rim), and the dancers' two stamps on the kick; all of these are hand claps and feet in the tradition. No bass, no chords.
dossier.lyrics: Chindau with Curtis's singing translation. Mostly vocables (eyo'we, we yo'we iye); the words proper: "Kwa'mai-we" (my mother's home), "Kwa'mai nda lega" (I left my mother's home), "Ndo da kwumisha" (I love my husband's home). Fit for class as a song about missing home. Curtis's own aside (women marry very young) is left out. Spelling to be checked by a Chindau speaker.
dossier.honesty: Traditional; the notes, words, accents and the four clap parts as Curtis printed them from C. Kamba Simango and other Ndau singers. Only the sounds of the layers are ours (in the tradition they are all hand claps).
dossier.licence: Natalie Curtis Burlin (d. 1921), Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent (G. Schirmer, 1920): public domain in the US and in Canada (Simango d. 1966, out of copyright under the life-plus-50 term then in force).
dossier.respect: A social dance song, nothing sacred. Credit C. Kamba Simango. The book's general framing ("Dark Continent", remarks on race) stays out of the record; Curtis's description of the dance and the clapping is kept.
dossier.review: A Chindau speaker, for the words; a teacher of southern African dance, for the stamps and the circle.

items.title: Mu-to-to-li'le
items.subtitle: Drip-drop the rain: Ndau children's song
items.source: Natalie Curtis Burlin, Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent (New York: G. Schirmer, 1920), Children's Songs I, p. 106 (game notes p. 30)

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent, at p. 106

items.blocked: Source check: compare with Curtis p. 106 (Children's Songs I), especially the sixteenths against the eighths (all of bars 2-4 are sixteenths but the last note) and the stress ticks. Ask someone who speaks Chindau to hear the words and the stresses before it is published.
items.notes: THE GAME (Curtis, p. 30): "This song is sung by children when playing in the rain. They call the raindrops to pour down till all the pools are full." They swim in the pools and spear the big red-breasted bullfrogs with little pointed sticks. "To-to" is the sound of rain falling in drops.

dossier.function: A rain game: children sing it while playing in the rain, calling the drops to fall until the pools are full, so they can swim, and hunt the big red-breasted bullfrogs. "To-to" is the sound of rain falling in drops (Curtis's note, from Simango).
dossier.elements: Four bars of 3/4 in quick sixteenths on four notes (E G A B), every bar opening "To-to li-le" with both syllables of "To-to" stressed: the stress falls on the pickup and on the downbeat, against the bar.
dossier.practice: Not fast (quarter = 60, Curtis). Sung by children, unaccompanied; the band rests. The stress ticks are part of the song: Curtis prints them over every "To" and "to".
dossier.honesty: Traditional; the notes, words and stress marks as Curtis printed them from C. Kamba Simango's singing. The English line is Curtis's singing translation, fitted to the same notes.
dossier.licence: Natalie Curtis Burlin (d. 1921), Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent (G. Schirmer, 1920): public domain in the US (published 1920) and in Canada (Curtis d. 1921; Simango, who gave the songs, d. 1966, so also out of copyright under the life-plus-50 term then in force).
dossier.respect: A children's game song, nothing sacred. Credit C. Kamba Simango, who brought the Ndau songs to the book. Take the notes and Curtis's game notes, not the book's general commentary, which has dated generalisations about race.
dossier.review: A Chindau speaker, for the words and the stresses.

items.title: Muvi'li, zu'ma, zu'ma
items.subtitle: Drying chant: Ndau children's game
items.source: Natalie Curtis Burlin, Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent (New York: G. Schirmer, 1920), Children's Songs III, p. 106 (game notes p. 31)

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent, at p. 106

items.blocked: Source check: compare with Curtis p. 106 (Children's Songs III). Classroom check: jump on each beat while chanting; does the one-line rhythm read well in the rhythm views, and should it live there rather than with the tunes?
items.notes: THE GAME (Curtis, p. 31): "After the children have been swimming, they jump up and down in the sun to shake the water off and dry themselves. They sing this little half-spoken song while jumping in time to each beat of the music." They think the song and the leaping are a kind of charm that helps make them dry.

dossier.function: A drying chant: after swimming the children jump up and down in the sun to shake the water off, chanting this and jumping on each beat; they hold the chant and the leaping to be a charm that dries them (Curtis, p. 31, from Simango).
dossier.elements: Rhythm only, spoken: twelve bars of 2/4 in eighths and quarters, the refrain "Mu-vi-li, zu-ma, zu-ma!" four times with "Ka-si-la" and "O-mai" between, each of those stressed on its first syllable.
dossier.practice: Rather quickly (quarter = 116, Curtis). Half spoken; one jump on each beat. The band plays only a soft low thump on the beat for the jumps; the notes are on one line because the chant has no pitch.
dossier.honesty: Traditional; the rhythm and words as Curtis printed them from C. Kamba Simango; the English line is Curtis's ("Bo-dy, bo-dy, dry off quick!"). The thump on the beat is ours.
dossier.licence: Natalie Curtis Burlin (d. 1921), Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent (G. Schirmer, 1920): public domain in the US and in Canada (Simango d. 1966, out of copyright under the life-plus-50 term then in force).
dossier.respect: A children's game, nothing sacred. Credit C. Kamba Simango. Leave out Curtis's remark beneath the plate comparing African and African-American accentuation; keep her game notes.
dossier.review: A Chindau speaker, for the words and stresses.

items.title: Na Bahia tem
items.subtitle: In Bahia there is: Brazilian sung dance in two lines
items.source: Alexina de Magalhães Pinto, Cantigas das creanças e do povo e danças populares (Rio de Janeiro: F. Alves, 1916), p. 15; the dance pp. 109-112

sourceUrls.label: Senado Federal digital library: Alexina de Magalhães Pinto, Cantigas das creanças e do povo e danças populares (1916), the original edition; the song at p. 15, the dance pp. 109-112

performances.label: children's roda version on YouTube (title checked, not yet listened to)

performanceNotes: The Senado Federal's 2023 re-edition of the same book (handle id/11111) includes a recording of this melody, 02_Na_Bahia.wav; its licence is not stated, so it is listed here, not linked. No archival recording by tradition-bearers found yet; the Museu do Folclore Edison Carneiro (Rio) and the Instituto Moreira Salles collections are the places to ask.
items.blocked: Source check: compare with Alexina p. 15 (the two sixteenths on "Seu bem", and the key signature: two sharps on the first staff, one on the second; the tune has no C, so they agree) and the dance version pp. 109-110, where small crosses mark the claps (the scan is faint there: the claps here follow her written description on p. 112). Still to transcribe: the dance version's polka section (pp. 109-110, from bar 16, with piano). A Portuguese speaker for the words; classroom check: the two facing lines, three steps and three claps forward, three back.
items.notes: THE DANCE (p. 112): "dispõem-se em duas fileiras, cada cavalheiro em frente á sua dama ... dão tres passos para a frente, batendo palmas tres vezes, uma em cada passo; (as palmas vão assignaladas na musica por uma cruzinha +) ... dão tres passos para traz." Then en avant and back again, a greeting, the traversez, and from bar 16 a polka in pairs.

dossier.function: A sung dance of two facing lines (dança cantada, em fileiras, ao som de palmas), from Rio, Bahia and Minas Gerais; in Minas, children danced it. The words name what "Bahia has": a penny coconut, a glass lamp, a flat-iron, a sewing machine; Bahia was the colony's first seat, where novelties came in (Alexina's note, after Sílvio Romero).
dossier.elements: 2/4, eight bars in two lines with a repeat; D major (the tune uses D E F# G A B, no C); a range of a sixth, D to B; eighths and quarters with one pair of sixteenths; the "tem, tem, tem" falls step by step (A G F# E), the second line answers it and ends on D.
dossier.practice: The dance (Alexina p. 112): two lines, each boy facing his partner about seven steps away. Bars 1-2, three steps forward, clapping on each step; bars 3-4, three steps back, singing and clapping; bars 5-6 forward again, 7-8 back. Then they greet each other and may cross over (traversez), the lines changing places; bars 9-16 forward and back again; from bar 16 everyone dances a polka in pairs to the end. One line can sing the first two lines and the other answer, all joining for the rest, and the forward-and-back can be replaced by other quadrille figures.
dossier.accompaniment: Tradition: hand claps by the dancers, marked with small crosses in Alexina's score (p. 109), three per two bars, one on each step; in the dance version a polka follows, which she gives with piano. The wider Bahian practice (samba de roda) adds the viola machete, pandeiro and scraped plate (prato e faca), per the UNESCO inscription of samba de roda; that is a different, adult setting and is not used here. Band here: claps only, three in every two bars on the steps (beats 1 and 2 of the first bar, beat 1 of the second). No bass, no chords; for the polka part, the band's march-and-polka style would be the stand-in. Needs nothing new for this part.
dossier.lyrics: Portuguese (1916 spelling: engommar, creanças). The score underlays "Na Bahia tem, tem, tem, tem, Na Bahia tem, seu bem, côco de vintém": "In Bahia there is, there is, there is, in Bahia there is, my dear, a penny coconut." Other verses (p. 111): "Na Bahia tem, vou mandar buscar lampeão de vidro, ó bahiana, ferro de engommar" (I'll send for a glass lamp, Bahian girl, and a flat-iron); "... machina de costura, seu bem, folle de soprar" (a sewing machine, my dear, a bellows). All fit for class. Alexina notes the verses are endless and that the ones sent with the dance were boasting challenge verses, which she leaves out; so do we.
dossier.honesty: Traditional; the tune, words and dance as Alexina de Magalhães Pinto printed them in 1916 (the tune "Rio, Bahia, Minas"; the dance as sent from Minas by Dr. G. Eutropio). The clap placement follows her description.
dossier.licence: Alexina de Magalhães Pinto (1870-1921), Cantigas das creanças e do povo e danças populares (Rio de Janeiro: Francisco Alves, 1916), Bibliotheca infantil: public domain in the US (1916), Canada and Brazil (d. 1921). The scan is published by the Senado Federal library under a Creative Commons licence; the notes here are read from it, not copied from the 2023 re-edition.
dossier.respect: The same words are sung in Umbanda as a ponto for the Baianos and the Erês (child spirits); this record is the children's dance from 1916, and a teacher may say so if asked. The book has a section of "cantigas dos pretos" whose dialect may caricature; nothing from it is used here.
dossier.review: A Portuguese speaker (Brazilian), for the words and the 1916 spellings; a Brazilian teacher who knows the roda, for the dance.

items.title: Pass the ball
items.subtitle: Jamaican ring game
items.source: Walter Jekyll (ed.), Jamaican Song and Story (London: David Nutt, 1907), Project Gutenberg #35410 (music as MusicXML), no. XCIV, p. 197

sourceUrls.label: Project Gutenberg #35410: Jamaican Song and Story, with page images and the music

items.blocked: Have a Jamaican culture bearer hear it with the mento band; the notes already match the 1907 plate.
items.notes: Words and tune as Jekyll printed them (Allegro). The ring closes up tight, shoulder to shoulder; hands behind the back pass the ball round and round, and the girl inside the ring tries to find it. The person with whom it is found goes into the ring and becomes the seeker.

dossier.function: game: a passing game in a closed ring (no dancing); hands behind backs pass a ball while the seeker in the middle tries to find it
dossier.elements: call and response by section; quavers on the words, a dotted crotchet on "round"; the melody falls by step to the tonic at each cadence
dossier.practice: Allegro, sung by everyone in the ring; the person found holding the ball becomes the seeker. "Goin'" is one short syllable, as Jekyll notes
dossier.honesty: arranged: the melody and words as Jekyll printed them; the mento backing (band, strum, rumba-box bass) is ours, in the idiom of Jamaican country bands
dossier.licence: public domain (published 1907; Project Gutenberg: for the use of anyone anywhere); notes converted from Gutenberg's MusicXML and checked bar by bar against its page image on 2026-11-10
dossier.respect: a children's game, for everyone; say it is Jamaican and that the words are Jamaican Patois
dossier.review: a Jamaican culture bearer (a teacher of Jamaican folk song, or the Jamaica Memory Bank / Louise Bennett's recordings) before publishing

items.title: Rāna jīnāk
items.subtitle: We have come to you: the Maghreb's opening song
items.source: Jules Rouanet, "La musique arabe dans le Maghreb", Lavignac, Encyclopédie de la musique, Part I vol. 5 (1922), p. 2824

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of Lavignac, Encyclopédie de la musique, Part I vol. 5 (1922), p. 2824 (Rouanet, "La musique arabe dans le Maghreb")
the page before (p. 2823): the festival procession and its instruments

performanceNotes: No recording found yet. Places to look: the Arab Music Archiving and Research foundation (AMAR); the 78s of Edmond Yafil's Algiers label on Gallica (gallica.bnf.fr); Algerian ʿaroubi and ḥawzi singers, who still open feasts with it. Listen before linking.
items.blocked: Source check: compare with Rouanet p. 2824 (the sixteenth run in bar 8, the second ending of the phrase in bar 15, and the accompaniment rhythm). An Arabic speaker who knows Algerian song (darja) to write the opening couplet in Arabic script and check the transliteration and meaning; Rouanet prints only the first words. Classroom check: as a hello song paired with B'qāw ʿala khēr (the goodbye song, its own record).
items.notes: THE PLATE: "Allegro", 2/4, no key signature, three staves with a repeat; words "Ra-na dji-nak, Ya dou-aï-ni, Ra-na dji-nak, Na-ri! Ya na-ri!" Below, "Rythme d'accompagnement": two lines of strokes, the upper (high) and lower (low), "etc."

dossier.function: The opening song of the Maghreb feast. Rouanet: "perhaps the best-known tune of the Maghreb"; it is played at religious and secular feasts alike, births, circumcisions, weddings, and the procession to a saint's tomb, and when the procession arrives the ghaitas play it again. The words greet the hosts: "We have come to you!", then wishes of joy and prosperity, the lines broken by the cry "My fire! O my fire!" (Rouanet's footnote 1).
dossier.elements: 2/4, Allegro; eighteen bars sung twice; final A, range G to e (a ninth); a dotted quarter and a sixteenth-note triplet that open each half, a run of eight sixteenths on "ni", and the answering cry "Na-ri! Ya na-ri!".
dossier.practice: Processional and festive: everyone knows it; the shawms (ghaita) and drums play it outdoors at the head of the procession; at home the women's ensemble plays it. In class: a hello song at the start of a lesson, sung as everyone arrives, with B'qāw at the end.
dossier.accompaniment: Tradition (Rouanet pp. 2823-2824, 2838): outdoors ghaita (shawm) with tbal (large two-headed drum) and naqqarat (small paired kettledrums); indoors the women's ensemble (messemaʿ) with kamanja (violin), tar (frame drum with jingles) and derbouka (goblet drum). Rouanet prints the "rythme d'accompagnement" under the tune: two strokes, high and low, in 2/4: high on sixteenths 1, 3, 5 and 8 (the 8th is the pickup he begins with), low on 1 and 5. Band here: high stroke on rim, low on bd, exactly his rhythm; no bass or chords (the music is unison, not harmonised). Needs: ghaita (GM shanai), tbal, naqqarat, derbouka.
dossier.lyrics: Rouanet prints only the opening words, "Rana djinak, ya dou aïni ... Nari! Ya nari!": tentatively رانا جيناك يا ضو عيني ... ناري يا ناري, "We have come to you, light of my eyes ... My fire! O my fire!" The rest of each couplet is improvised good wishes (footnote 1). Fit for class. The full couplet, and the Arabic script above, wait for an Arabic speaker (see review).
dossier.honesty: Traditional, anonymous; the notes, the words as far as printed, and the drum rhythm are Rouanet's transcription (1920). The band plays his rhythm on stand-in sounds.
dossier.licence: Jules Rouanet (1858-1944), "La musique arabe dans le Maghreb", in Lavignac and La Laurencie (eds.), Encyclopédie de la musique et dictionnaire du Conservatoire, Part I vol. 5 (Paris: Delagrave, 1922; the section dated "Copyright by Librairie Delagrave, 1920"): public domain in the US (published before 1931) and in Canada (Rouanet d. 1944).
dossier.respect: The tune also leads processions to saints' tombs, where the first verse of the Qur'an is recited aloud (Rouanet p. 2824); the song itself is not a religious text. Rouanet writes as a French colonial musicologist in Algiers; the record quotes his facts about the music, not his framing.
dossier.review: An Arabic speaker familiar with Algerian song, for the words; ideally an Algerian musician, for the tempo and the drum strokes.

items.title: Resvelons nous
items.subtitle: Wake up, lovers: a May song with a canon burden
items.source: J. F. R. and C. Stainer, Dufay and his Contemporaries (London: Novello, 1898), pp. 132-133, from Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Canonici misc. 213

sourceUrls.label: IMSLP: Stainer, Dufay and his Contemporaries (1898), the full scan; the song is at pp. 132-133 (pdf pp. 170-171)
HathiTrust: another full-view scan of the same book

items.blocked: Source check: hear all three voices against Stainer pp. 132-133 (IMSLP #344705, pdf pp. 170-171), especially the editorial accidentals (Stainer's sharps and flats over the notes) and the burden's last three bars, which leave the canon. Then classroom check: can a class hold the burden as a two-part round, an octave up, while the teacher sings the top line?
items.notes: THE WORDS (top voice): "Resvelons nous, resvelons, amoureux; / Alons au bois tantost en cilir le may. / Et chanterons chascun un virelay / Pour sa dame: s'en serons plus joieux." Wake up, wake up, lovers; let us go to the woods now to gather the may, and each of us will sing a virelai for his lady, and be the happier for it. The burden: "Alons ent bien tos au may", let's be off to the may.

dossier.function: A May-morning song: wake up, lovers, and go to the woods to gather the may (green boughs and blossom brought home on May Day). The burden underneath is the company's own call, "Alons ent bien tos au may", let's be off to the may.
dossier.elements: A five-bar burden sung as a canon: the contratenor sings it, the tenor answers a fifth lower one bar later, each resting a bar before going round again. Over it a solo top line in 3/2. Cadences on D with the open fifth D-A.
dossier.practice: Two groups sing the burden as a round, the second group starting one bar after the first (an octave up for children's voices); a soloist or the teacher sings the top line. The burden alone is a first canon: seven notes, stepwise, a five-bar loop. The band rests; the three voices are the whole piece.
dossier.honesty: Composed, not traditional: Guillaume Du Fay, before about 1436 (the date by which it was copied into Oxford, Bodleian Library, Canonici misc. 213). The notes are Stainer's 1898 transcription, note values halved, with his editorial accidentals.
dossier.licence: Stainer, Dufay and his Contemporaries (London: Novello, 1898): public domain in the US (published 1898) and in Canada (the editors died 1901, 1937 and 1939). Notes read from the IMSLP scan of the Sibley Music Library copy.
dossier.respect: A secular spring song; nothing sacred or sensitive.
dossier.review: An early-music singer or choir director, for the editorial accidentals and the tempo.

items.title: Sakura
items.subtitle: Japanese koto song
items.source: Daisyfield.com transcription (Tom Potter, 2008, donated to the public domain) (koto version; the source book is not named on the page)

sourceUrls.label: Daisyfield transcription (PDF)

items.notes: Words in romaji (old text: yayoi no sora wa, miwatasu kagiri...). The scale is the in scale on A, A B flat D E F; the band holds A and E (A5) and plays no drums.

dossier.function: song for the koto: cherry blossom in spring; taught in Japanese schools since the Meiji era
dossier.elements: in (miyako-bushi) scale on A (A B flat D E F), here a fifth below the usual school key; 4/4; the band holds an open fifth A and E, quietly, as a koto's open strings might
dossier.practice: slow and even; a koto plays the melody with plucked ornaments; no percussion (the band is kept at low energy)
dossier.honesty: arranged: the koto melody as Daisyfield transcribed it, words in romaji; the drone is ours

dossier.review: a Japanese culture bearer or a teacher of min'yo or koto before publishing

items.title: Vámonos por Santa Anita
items.subtitle: Come, let's go to Santa Anita: Mexican play song
items.source: Eleanor Hague, Spanish-American Folk-Songs, Memoirs of the American Folk-Lore Society 10 (1917), No. 75, p. 98

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of Hague, Spanish-American Folk-Songs (1917), at p. 98

items.blocked: Source check: compare with Hague No. 75, p. 98 (the dotted-eighth and sixteenth figures in every beat). Classroom check: can a class keep the dotted figure long-short, not even, at a gay tempo?
items.notes: THE PLATE: "Gayly", 2/4 in G major, two lines of four bars with the same notes, Spanish words with Hague's English under them: "Come, let's go to Santa Anita! Come, let's go! for there you'll find / In the lead the wagons harnessed, And the oxen on behind."

dossier.function: A light play song from northern Mexico: come, let's go to Santa Anita (a village outing), the oxcarts in front and the oxen behind.
dossier.elements: G major, 2/4, four bars sung twice; every beat but the last is a dotted eighth and a sixteenth, a skipping long-short figure; a range of a ninth (D above middle C to the E an octave higher).
dossier.practice: Gayly (Hague). The skipping figure suits skipping or a walking game in pairs; the second line of words takes the same four bars.
dossier.honesty: Traditional; the notes, Spanish words and English singing translation as Hague printed them from Mrs. Karbe's singing.
dossier.licence: Eleanor Hague (1875-1954), Spanish-American Folk-Songs, Memoirs of the American Folk-Lore Society 10 (1917): public domain in the US and in Canada (Hague d. 1954).
dossier.respect: A play song; nothing sacred or sensitive.
dossier.review: A Spanish-speaking teacher, for the words.

items.title: Xianhua diao (鮮花調)
items.subtitle: The fresh flower: Chinese popular song, two early versions
items.source: J. A. van Aalst, Chinese Music (Shanghai, 1884), p. 19; John Barrow, Travels in China (London, 1804), p. 316, as taken down by J. C. Hüttner

sourceUrls.label: van Aalst, Chinese Music (1884), p. 19: "Song called 鮮花 (The Fresh Beautiful Flower)", staff and gongche
van Aalst p. 16: his table of the gongche note names
Barrow, Travels in China (1804), p. 316: "Moo-lee-wha", with stanza I (stanza II and the literal translation on p. 317)

performances.label: Harvard, Sounding China: the Barrow and Hüttner tune and its early European history (with performances)
Zhang Ye, Jiangsu folk song broadcast: the modern (1957) "Mo li hua", for comparison, not this text or tune exactly (title checked, not yet listened to)

performanceNotes: Wanted: a Jiangsu or Yangzhou xiaodiao singer, or a sizhu ensemble, singing Xianhua diao in the older form; Berthold Laufer's 1901 cylinders from Shanghai (Indiana University Archives of Traditional Music) are the earliest recordings of the region's songs.
items.blocked: Source check: van Aalst p. 19 (staff and gongche agree; check bar 11's last note B and the old-style quarter rests) and Barrow p. 316 (bars 9-11 and 13, and the last bar, printed as a dotted half). A Chinese speaker to confirm the characters behind Barrow's romanization and to fit stanza I to one of the two melodies (neither source prints the words under the notes). Engine: the band wants a heterophony part (the tune itself on a second instrument, ornamented) before this sounds like the tradition.
items.notes: VAN AALST'S GONGCHE (p. 19), read top to bottom, right to left, with his gamut (p. 16: 合 C, 四 D (printed 士), 上 F, 尺 G, 工 A, 凡 B, 六 c, 五 d; dots after a note lengthen it, a circle marks the fourth beat): 工· 工 六 五 凡 凡 五。 六·· 五 六。 (twice) | 工· 六· 六· 五 凡。 六·· 五 六。 工·· 尺 六 工 尺。 上·· 尺 上。 工·· 上· 尺·。 六·· 五 六。 尺·· 工 尺 上 合。 士·· 上·· 尺· 工 士。 六·· 凡 五 六 工 尺。 六···. It agrees with his staff note for note, which settles the staff's two lowest notes (合 C and 士 D).

dossier.function: A popular song (xiaodiao) of the lower Yangzi, sung for entertainment by a solo singer who often accompanied herself or himself; Barrow heard it in Canton and calls it "one of the most popular songs in the whole country"; van Aalst prints it as a popular song a century later. Its words praise a fresh flower, the jasmine (moli), too lovely to pick.
dossier.elements: Pentatonic (F G A c d in van Aalst, the gong mode on F with B natural, 凡, as a passing tone; G A B d e in Barrow, the gong mode on G), both ending on the fifth degree (zhi); 4/4 in eighths and quarters with a dotted quarter at each half-line; van Aalst C to d (a ninth), Barrow D to g (an eleventh).
dossier.practice: Sung solo, unhurried, the singer ornamenting the line; the instruments play the same tune together, each a little differently (heterophony), never in chords (Barrow p. 315; van Aalst p. 36). In class: sing or play van Aalst's version (smaller range) on the recorder; then hear Barrow's and find what changed.
dossier.accompaniment: Tradition: Barrow (p. 315) heard the singer accompany himself "with a kind of guitar" (a pipa or sanxian); Chinese bands play "in unison, and sometimes an instrument takes the octave", never in parts. Van Aalst (p. 36): the popular band is two pipa (played by girls who also sing), sanxian, one or two fiddles (erhu, huqin), a small drum beating time, flute (dizi) and yangqin, all on the melody. Band here: only a clapper (wood block) on the first beat of each bar, standing in for the ban or small drum; no bass, no chords, because the music has none. Needs: a heterophony part (the tune on a second sound with ornaments), and dizi, erhu, pipa, yangqin sounds; until then, a teacher can play the tune on the recorder with the class singing.
dossier.lyrics: Barrow prints two stanzas in 1790s romanization with a word-by-word translation (p. 317). Our reading of the characters (tentative, for a Chinese speaker to confirm): I. 好一朵鮮花，有朝一日落在我家，我本待不出門，對着鮮花兒樂。 "How delightful this branch of fresh flowers! One morning it fell into my house. I, the owner, will not go out; I will sit with the fresh flower and be happy." II. 好一朵茉莉花，滿園花開賽不過它，我本待採一朵戴，又恐看花人兒罵。 "How delightful this jasmine flower! In the full garden no flower excels it. I would pick one to wear, but fear the flower's keeper would scold." Both fit for class. Not underlaid: neither source sets the words to the notes. Not the 1957 He Fang text and tune ("好一朵美丽的茉莉花"), which is in copyright.
dossier.honesty: Traditional. Van Aalst's version as he printed it in staff notation and gongche (they agree); Barrow's as Johann Christian Hüttner took it down "in its unadorned state". The clapper on the downbeat is ours.
dossier.licence: J. A. van Aalst (1858-after 1914), Chinese Music (Shanghai: Inspectorate General of Customs, 1884); John Barrow (1764-1848), Travels in China (London: Cadell and Davies, 1804), tune taken down by Hüttner (d. 1847): both public domain in the US and Canada.
dossier.respect: Barrow and van Aalst write as outsiders who often dismiss Chinese music (Barrow's "aggregation of harsh sounds"); the record keeps their facts and transcriptions only. The tune became a political symbol in 2011 (the "Jasmine Revolution" calls); not something to raise in class unless asked.
dossier.review: A Chinese speaker for the characters and the singing; ideally a musician who plays Jiangnan sizhu, for the ornaments.

items.title: Zdravets
items.subtitle: Geranium: Bulgarian horo song in 9/16
items.source: Vasil Stoin, Narodna pesnopoyka (Sofia, 1930), No. 102 "Zdravets", p. 98

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of Stoin, Narodna pesnopoyka (1930), at p. 98, No. 102

performances.label: CREM-CNRS catalogue entry for the Serbian variant (metadata only)

performanceNotes: No recording of this Bulgarian song was found. A Serbian variant, "Zdravche, venche, beru li te mome?" (Orljane, Serbia, recorded by Radmila Petrović, Radio Belgrade 1981), is in the CREM-CNRS archive (CNRSMH_E_1988_011_001_014), listening restricted. The Bulgarian National Radio folklore archive is the place to ask for a Bulgarian one.
items.blocked: Source check: compare with Stoin No. 102, p. 98 (bar 3 of each line, the slurs, and the repeat marks at the line ends). A Bulgarian speaker to check the modern spelling, the stresses and the translation. Classroom check: count 9 as 2+2+2+3 with Stoin's syllables, then dance a simple horo step to it.
items.notes: THE WORDS (Stoin, modern spelling): "Здравче, венче, берат ли те моми?" / "Та мене ли моми да не берат? / Като цъфтя, все гора мирише. / Като дойде на ден на Гергьовден, / те си дойдат хубави девойки, / та ме берат във нови цедила, / та ме носят на бързи потоци, / та ме вият на зелени венци / и ме турят на вакли агънца."

dossier.function: A horo song: sung while dancing the horo, the line dance of Bulgarian village festivities. A question and its answer: "Little geranium, little wreath, do the girls pick you?" and the geranium tells how the girls pick it on St George's Day, weave it into wreaths and crown the lambs. Zdravets (Geranium macrorrhizum) carries the word for health, zdrave, and is given for health at feasts.
dossier.elements: 9/16 in the grouping 2+2+2+3 (quick-quick-quick-slow), the daychovo horo's metre; two three-bar lines, each a ten-syllable verse line; final A with B flat above it, a range of a sixth (F to d).
dossier.practice: Fast (Stoin: Бързо). Horo songs were sung by two groups of women, one at each end of the dance line, answering each other line by line; instruments came in after the singing. In class, two halves of the room take alternate lines while the rest step the horo: count "1 2 3 4-a" (Stoin's pp. 243-245 count uneven metres with syllables).
dossier.accompaniment: Tradition: the horo is first sung unaccompanied by the two groups (see practice); played horos use gaida (bagpipe with a drone), kaval (rim-blown flute), gadulka (bowed fiddle), tambura (long-necked lute) and tapan (two-headed drum, a heavy beater on one head and a thin switch on the other). Sources: Stoin's heading "Пѣе се на хоро" (sung at the horo); for the instruments and the singing groups, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_of_Bulgaria (to be replaced by an ethnography). Band here: the tapan only, the heavy beater (bd) on the first beat and the switch (rim) on the other three, one bar of 2+2+2+3; and a held A on the bass as a stand-in for the gaida's drone. Needs: tapan, gaida (GM bagpipe), kaval, gadulka.
dossier.lyrics: All of Stoin's words are fit for class: the question, then eight lines of answer, sung two lines to each pass of the tune (five passes). Written here in modern Bulgarian spelling (Stoin uses the pre-1945 spelling: вѣнче, бератъ), with a transliteration and our English translation; to be checked by a Bulgarian speaker. "Вакли агънца" are lambs with dark rings round the eyes.
dossier.honesty: Traditional, no composer named (Stoin's book also has composed school songs; No. 102 is not one of them). Notes and words as Stoin printed them. The tapan pattern and the drone are ours, after the practice described above; turn the band off to hear the song as the singers sang it.
dossier.licence: Vasil Stoin (1880-1938), Narodna pesnopoyka (Sofia: Ministry of Education, 1930): public domain in the US (published 1930; PD from 1 January 2026) and in Canada and Bulgaria (Stoin d. 1938).
dossier.respect: St George's Day (Gergyovden, 6 May) is a Christian and folk feast; the garlanded lamb is the feast's sacrificed lamb (kurban). That is a fact a teacher may give or leave; the song itself is about flowers, girls and lambs.
dossier.review: A Bulgarian speaker, for the spelling, stresses and translation; a Bulgarian dance teacher, for the horo step.
